name: Through the Looking-Glass
lines: Through the Looking-Glass
Through the Looking-Glass: Alice's drawing-room, Looking-Glass House, the garden of live flowers, and the great chessboard country, square by square, to the Eighth Square and the feast
Alice's house in the snow

about ten inches high

your own right size
Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass (1871)
The gentleman dressed in white paper
A voice in the carriage
Oh, what fun it'll be, when they see me through the glass in here, and can't get at me!
Those kittens have had the worsted all over the hearth-rug again, Miss Alice.
Where do you come from? And where are you going? Look up, speak nicely, and don't twiddle your fingers all the time.
Bread-and-butter, bread-and-butter... I've been a-dressing myself for the last two hours.
I see nobody on the road. ... I only wish I had such eyes.
It's my own invention.
Ahoy! Ahoy! Check! You're my prisoner!
If you think we're wax-works, you ought to pay, you know.
Contrariwise, if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn't, it ain't. That's logic.
Tickets, please! ... You're travelling the wrong way.
I beg pardon, your Majesty, I hadn't quite finished my tea when I was sent for.
The butter's spread too thick!
When I use a word, it means just what I choose it to mean, neither more nor less.
What is it you want to buy?
She ought to know her way to the ticket-office, even if she doesn't know her alphabet!
She'll have to go back from here as luggage!
What sort of insects do you rejoice in, where YOU come from?
What do you call yourself? ... I'll tell you, if you'll come a little further on.
I'm just out of breath. You never saw such a cloud of dust!
What's this! Are you animal, or vegetable, or mineral?
I always thought children were fabulous monsters! Is it alive?
What is it, now? Wexes it?
Kitty, the black kitten
Snowdrop, the white kitten
The monstrous crow
The White Knight's horse
The Red Knight's horse
The time has come to talk of many things.
Did you hear the volcano?
We can talk, when there's anybody worth talking to.
A boy with an armful of sticks
We're getting in sticks for the bonfire, miss. It wants plenty of sticks, Miss Alice!
Another boy, blowing on his fingers
It's that cold! The snow's coming down ever so thick.
The front door of Alice's house
The looking-glass over the chimney-piece
climb up and go through the glass
🪞 The glass melts away like a bright silvery mist. You jump lightly down into the Looking-glass room.
The front door of Looking-Glass House
I never saw anybody that looked stupider.
Mind your manners!
She's coming! I hear her footstep, thump, thump, thump, along the gravel-walk!
The garden path, twisting like a corkscrew
🌀 The path twists like a corkscrew. Whichever way you follow it, it brings you back to the house door.
The top of the little hill
look out over the country
♟️ Marked out just like a large chessboard. Little brooks run straight across it from side to side, and little green hedges divide the ground into squares.
The Looking-glass room
'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.
The hall of Looking-Glass House
Up the stairs to the Looking-glass room
A farmer in a smock
Everything's backwards here, you know. We plant the harvest and reap the seed.
The cows give the milk back, of an evening.
Mind the hedge, miss: it's a file, and you mustn't cross it unless you're a Knight.
The tree at the end of the Second Square
🌳 Under the same tree. Everything is just as it was: here you must run as fast as you can to keep in the same place.
The train at the Looking-Glass platform
🚂 A railway carriage.
The great flowers of the Third Square
look at the elephants
🐘 Elephants! Going about among the flowers, poking their proboscis into them, sucking out the honey. And what enormous flowers they must be!
The Looking-Glass insects in the tree

🦋 The Looking-Glass insects. A Rocking-horse-fly, swinging from branch to branch; a Snap-dragon-fly with a raisin burning in brandy for its head; a Bread-and-butter-fly with wings of bread-and-butter.
The wood where things have no names
🌲 This must be the wood where things have no names. It is very cool and shady under the trees, and you cannot for the life of you remember what anything is called.
TO TWEEDLEDUM'S HOUSE
TO THE HOUSE OF TWEEDLEDEE
The two finger-posts
☝️ Two finger-posts, pointing the same way. TO TWEEDLEDUM'S HOUSE and TO THE HOUSE OF TWEEDLEDEE. "I do believe they live in the same house!"
A rattle, lying under the tree
🪇 A nice new rattle. Or it was, before it was spoiled.
The sea-shore of the poem
🌊 The sun was shining on the sea, shining with all his might. The sands are wet as wet can be; the oysters lie in their beds.
A railway carriage
EGGS, WOOL, NEEDLES AND ALL MANNER OF CURIOUS THINGS
The door of the little dark shop
The boat in the river
look at the rushes
🚣 The scented rushes. The dearest rushes are always the ones out of reach; they begin to fade, and lose their scent, the moment they are picked.
A woman with a basket
They've been at it all morning. Round and round the town, for the crown.
A baker in his apron
White bread, brown bread, and plum-cake, all ready for when they've done.
An old man on a bench
The Lion beat the Unicorn all round the town, same as the song says.
A girl with a hoop
They drummed them out of town last time!
When it's done, we drum them out.
The arched doorway: QUEEN ALICE
The Visitors' Bell
🔔 The Visitors' Bell. Nobody comes. "I'm not a visitor, and I'm not a servant. There OUGHT to be one marked 'Queen,' you know."
The Servants' Bell
🔔 The Servants' Bell. It rings, a long way inside.

A little White Pawn

The fourth of November, 1871, late in the afternoon, and snowing. Alice is curled up in the great arm-chair in the drawing-room, half talking to herself and half asleep, with the black kitten in her lap; and you are the dreamer by the fire, listening.
Hush. The volcano.
Two and two, and keep to your squares.
Arm in arm, if you please.
We walk arm in arm, two and two.
I turned cold to the very ends of my whiskers!
I MUST get a thinner pencil.
My precious Lily! My imperial kitten!
Lily, the little White Pawn
(she squeaks and kicks)
🐈 The way Dinah washed her children's faces
Come and sit by the great arm-chair, where Alice is curled up with the black kitten
Alice is winding up the ball of worsted, and the kitten is helping: listen
🧶 The black kitten and the worsted
The worsted is all over the hearth-rug, in knots and tangles: gather the balls up for Alice
Alice catches up the kitten and gives it a little kiss: listen
😾 Oh, you wicked little thing!
Alice settles back with the kitten and the worsted: listen
🔥 Do you know what to-morrow is, Kitty?
Go up into the window and look out at the snow, where the boys were getting in sticks
Look out of the window: the boys have left a great heap of sticks at the end of the lane, and given up for the snow. What is to-morrow, that they want so many?
The bonfire: the fifth of November, Guy Fawkes Day
A wedding in the church
I was watching the boys getting in sticks for the bonfire—and it wants plenty of sticks, Kitty!
Alice holds up one finger and tells the kitten all its faults: listen
☝️ Number one, number two, number three
☝️ The second fault
What was Kitty's fault number two?
It squeaked twice while Dinah was washing its face
It pulled Snowdrop away by the tail just as Alice had put down the saucer of milk before her
It unwound every bit of the worsted
That was number one.
That was number three.
you pulled Snowdrop away by the tail just as I had put down the saucer of milk before her!
Alice talks on, more to herself than the kitten
Alice is saving up all the kitten's punishments for Wednesday week. If her own punishments were saved up, and each one was going without a dinner, what does she think?
She would be very hungry and cry
She would have to go without fifty dinners at once, and she would far rather go without them than eat them
She would be sent to bed
I'd far rather go without them than eat them!
Alice listens to the snow against the window-panes
❄️ Do you hear the snow against the window-panes, Kitty?
Stand in the window a little, and listen to the snow kissing the panes, as Alice says
Come to the chess-table, where Alice and the kitten were playing
Alice asks Kitty seriously whether it can play chess
♟️ Kitty, can you play chess?
Alice's favourite phrase is "Let's pretend". When she once pretended something to her old nurse, shouting suddenly in her ear, what was it?
That she was a hungry hyaena, and the nurse was a bone
That she was the Queen of England
That the house was on fire
Nurse! Do let's pretend that I'm a hungry hyaena, and you're a bone.
Alice wants the Red Queen off the chess-table, for the kitten to sit up and copy: find a piece fallen under the table and bring it
Alice sets the Red Queen up before the kitten as a model
👑 Let's pretend that you're the Red Queen, Kitty!
Come to the chimney-piece, where Alice holds the kitten up to the looking-glass
Alice tells Kitty all her ideas about Looking-glass House: listen
🪞 The bit behind the fireplace
Look into the glass over the chimney-piece. The room in it is just the same as the drawing-room, only the things go the other way. Which bit of it can Alice never see, and wants to see so much?
The bit behind the fireplace, to know whether they have a fire in the winter
The carpet under the sofa
I can see all of it when I get upon a chair—all but the bit behind the fireplace.
Alice is up on the chimney-piece, and the glass is beginning to melt away
✨ Let's pretend the glass has got all soft like gauze
The glass is melting away like a bright silvery mist: climb up after Alice and go through
🪞 Through the glass
Look whether there is a fire in the fireplace here
🕰️ The pictures are alive, and the clock grins
Look up at the clock on the chimney-piece (it has the face of a little old man) and at the pictures beside the fire: their eyes follow you
♟️ The chessmen were walking about, two and two!
Kneel down by the hearth and watch the chessmen walking among the cinders: say good evening to the Castles
The Castles walk arm in arm, and do not seem to hear you. You are invisible to them, as Alice is.
👑 Here are the Red King and the Red Queen
🔊 Squeaking on the table
The White Queen rushes past the King, knocking him over among the cinders
😱 It is the voice of my child!
The White King sits up among the cinders, rubbing his nose
👐 Lily is screaming herself into a fit
The White Queen is trying to clamber up the side of the fender to her child. Alice is very anxious to be of use. What does she do?
Shouts to the Queen to climb the poker
Picks up the Queen and sets her on the table by the side of her noisy little daughter
Picks up Lily and puts her in the hearth
she hastily picked up the Queen and set her on the table by the side of her noisy little daughter.
🌋 Mind the volcano!
Watch the White King struggle slowly up from bar to bar of the fender
🧗 You'll be hours and hours getting to the table
Alice offers to help him up. The King takes no notice. What does Alice do, and what happens to the King's face?
She picks him up very gently and lifts him across, but first dusts him, for he is covered with ashes; and he makes such a face
She calls the Queen
🧹 She dusts him a little, and he makes such a face that she nearly drops him for laughing.
🫨 He turned cold to the very ends of his whiskers
Come to the work-table and look on while the King takes out his enormous memorandum-book
✏️ Alice takes hold of the end of the pencil
✏️ What did Alice write?
Alice was too strong for the King, and wrote in his memorandum-book for him. What did she put?
THE WHITE QUEEN IS ASLEEP
THE WHITE KNIGHT IS SLIDING DOWN THE POKER. HE BALANCES VERY BADLY
A VOLCANO BLEW ME UP
That was the Queen's.
📖 A book lying near Alice on the table
📖 It was like this.
🪞 A Looking-glass book
The book is all in some language Alice does not know. How can she read it?
Turn it upside down
Hold it up to a glass, and the words will all go the right way again
Read it with one eye shut
Why, it's a Looking-glass book, of course!
Carry the book to the glass over the chimney-piece and hold it up, so that the words go the right way
📜 This was the poem that Alice read.
📜 'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
📜 Beware the Jabberwock, my son!
⚔️ The vorpal sword
Read on. What does the young hero take in hand to go after the manxome foe?
He rests by the Tumtum tree.
He took his vorpal sword in hand:
🔥 The Jabberwock, with eyes of flame
🎉 O frabjous day!
📜 'Twas brillig, again
That the Jabberwock won
SOMEBODY killed SOMETHING: that's clear, at any rate
🏃 Down the stairs
